title: Endocrinology — Adrenal Disorders, CAH, Puberty & DSD

calc_items.title: Height velocity
calc_items.question: Height is 117.2 cm and 8 months later 121.6 cm. Calculate the annualised height velocity.

calc_items.title: Corrected age
calc_items.question: An infant born at 30 weeks' gestation is now 20 weeks old (chronological age). Calculate the corrected age.

calc_items.title: Body surface area
calc_items.question: Height 120 cm, weight 25 kg. Calculate the Mosteller body surface area √(height × weight / 3600).

calc_items.title: Glucose-corrected sodium
calc_items.question: Measured sodium 128 mmol/L with glucose 500 mg/dL. Using +1.6 mmol/L per 100 mg/dL of glucose above 100, estimate the corrected sodium.
calc_items.working: 128 + 1.6 × (500 − 100)/100 = 134.4 mmol/L. An exam arithmetic exercise with the stated convention; clinical protocols use different factors, and effective osmolality and trends guide decisions.

calc_items.title: BMI
calc_items.question: Height 1.35 m, weight 32 kg. Calculate the BMI.
calc_items.working: 32/1.35² = 17.56 kg/m²; interpret on the age/sex percentile chart.

2.B: 11-deoxycortisol rises in 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency; in 21-hydroxylase deficiency the block lies before it, so 11-deoxycortisol is low.
2.C: Cortisol is the deficient end product in classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency, not an accumulating precursor.
2.D: Adrenal androgens such as DHEAS and androstenedione may rise from shunting, but 17-OHP is the characteristic diagnostic marker; DHEAS alone is not.

3.A: High sodium with low potassium suggests mineralocorticoid excess (e.g. 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency), the opposite of aldosterone deficiency in salt-wasting CAH.
3.B: Aldosterone deficiency causes renal sodium loss, so sodium falls; hypernatraemia with hyperkalaemia does not fit salt wasting.
3.C: Hypokalaemia indicates mineralocorticoid excess; salt-wasting CAH impairs potassium excretion and causes hyperkalaemia with hyponatraemia.

4.A: 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes virilisation but with salt wasting or normal blood pressure, since mineralocorticoid synthesis is impaired rather than excessive.
4.B: 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency causes hypertension but with sex-steroid deficiency, i.e. sexual infantilism or undervirilised 46,XY, not virilisation.
4.D: Aromatase deficiency causes maternal and 46,XX virilisation from unconverted androgens but does not produce mineralocorticoid excess or hypertension.

5.A: 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes androgen excess and salt wasting, not hypertension with low sex steroids.
5.C: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency impairs DHT formation, causing 46,XY undervirilisation, but adrenal steroidogenesis and blood pressure are normal.
5.D: Androgen insensitivity has normal or high androgen production with receptor resistance and no hypertension.

6.B: Testes develop only with a Y chromosome/SRY; a 46,XX infant with CAH has ovaries, and the uterus persists without testicular AMH.
6.C: Testes are not present in 46,XX CAH; virilisation is from adrenal androgens acting on external genitalia, while gonads remain ovaries.
6.D: Gonads and Mullerian structures are normal in 46,XX CAH; only the external genitalia are virilised by adrenal androgen.

7.A: 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency is the second most common form, accounting for roughly 5-8% of CAH.
7.B: 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency is a rare form of CAH.
7.C: 3-beta-HSD deficiency is a rare form of CAH, far less frequent than 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

10.B: Secondary adrenal insufficiency results from ACTH deficiency, so ACTH would be low or inappropriately normal, not high.
10.C: Cushing syndrome features cortisol excess, not low morning cortisol.
10.D: Exogenous glucocorticoids suppress ACTH; measured endogenous cortisol may be low but ACTH is low, not high.

11.A: Primary adrenal failure removes cortisol feedback, so ACTH is high, not low.
11.B: Primary hyperaldosteronism is autonomous aldosterone excess with suppressed renin; it does not cause low ACTH and low cortisol.
11.C: 21-hydroxylase excess is not a recognised entity; 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes low cortisol with high ACTH.

12.A: Aldosterone regulates sodium and potassium handling and has no melanocortin effect on skin pigmentation.
12.B: Insulin excess is linked to acanthosis nigricans, not the diffuse hyperpigmentation of Addison disease.
12.D: Growth hormone does not cause hyperpigmentation; Addison pigmentation reflects high ACTH/POMC peptides acting on MC1R.

13.A: Exogenous glucocorticoids suppress, rather than increase, ACTH secretion; high ACTH would protect against adrenal atrophy.
13.C: Renin is regulated mainly by volume and sodium, and the renin-aldosterone axis is largely preserved in glucocorticoid-induced suppression.
13.D: Adrenal androgen excess is not the mechanism; suppression arises from feedback inhibition of CRH and ACTH causing adrenal atrophy.

14.B: Bedside glucose is appropriate because hypoglycaemia is common in adrenal crisis, especially in children.
14.C: Restoring intravascular volume with isotonic fluid is a core step in managing the shock of adrenal crisis.
14.D: Hypoglycaemia must be corrected promptly with dextrose alongside parenteral hydrocortisone.

16.A: A random daytime cortisol is unreliable because of diurnal variation and stress; screening uses late-night salivary cortisol, urinary free cortisol or dexamethasone suppression.
16.B: Sodium is neither sensitive nor specific for hypercortisolism and cannot screen for Cushing syndrome.
16.D: ACTH is used after hypercortisolism is confirmed to distinguish ACTH-dependent from independent causes, not as a screening test.

17.A: Constitutional tall stature involves normal or high height velocity, not growth deceleration.
17.C: Exogenous obesity usually accompanies normal or increased height velocity and often advanced bone age; deceleration with weight gain points to cortisol excess.
17.D: Familial short stature shows short but normal-velocity growth parallel to centiles, without disproportionate weight gain.

18.B: Exogenous glucocorticoids feed back to suppress ACTH; markedly elevated ACTH suggests ACTH-dependent Cushing disease or ectopic ACTH.
18.C: Primary aldosterone excess is a separate mineralocorticoid disorder and is not caused by exogenous glucocorticoids.
18.D: Endogenous cortisol is usually suppressed in iatrogenic Cushing syndrome, because the HPA axis is inhibited.

20.A: Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism and has no mineralocorticoid activity.
20.B: Desmopressin is a vasopressin analogue for central diabetes insipidus; it does not promote renal sodium retention or potassium excretion.
20.D: Somatropin is recombinant growth hormone and has no role in mineralocorticoid replacement.

21.A: Salt-wasting CAH tends to cause hyperkalaemia, so routine potassium supplementation is inappropriate.
21.C: Potassium-sparing diuretics worsen sodium loss and hyperkalaemia, the very problem in aldosterone deficiency.
21.D: Electrolytes, with renin, are needed to titrate fludrocortisone and salt supplements; omitting monitoring is unsafe.

22.B: HbA1c reflects glycaemic control and does not gauge mineralocorticoid adequacy.
22.C: TSH assesses thyroid function and is unrelated to fludrocortisone dosing.
22.D: IGF-1 reflects growth hormone status, not mineralocorticoid replacement.

23.A: Glucocorticoid excess suppresses growth; accelerated height velocity suggests under-treatment with androgen excess.
23.B: CAH is a lifelong genetic enzyme defect; no glucocorticoid dose cures it, and excess only adds iatrogenic harm.
23.C: Excess glucocorticoid suppresses ACTH; high ACTH indicates under-replacement.

24.A: Low blood pressure points to mineralocorticoid or salt deficiency, not to inadequate suppression of adrenal androgens.
24.B: Hypoglycaemia reflects cortisol deficiency or intercurrent stress and is not a marker of androgen excess.
24.D: Suppressed ACTH with Cushingoid features indicates glucocorticoid over-treatment, the opposite of under-treatment.

25.A: Ovarian oestrogen feminises rather than virilises, and the androgen excess in 21-hydroxylase deficiency arises in the adrenal cortex, present even in 46,XY infants.
25.C: Prolactin excess causes galactorrhoea and hypogonadism, not virilisation; it plays no role in the steroidogenic block of 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
25.D: Thyroid hormone is not part of adrenal steroidogenesis and its excess causes thyrotoxicosis, not genital virilisation.

27.A: Wolffian ducts are maintained by testosterone in 46,XY fetuses; they regress in the absence of testosterone, not because of AMH.
27.B: AMH has no role in adrenal cortex development; the fetal adrenal zone involutes postnatally independent of AMH.
27.C: AMH is a testicular product in 46,XY development and causes Müllerian regression; it does not drive ovarian follicle development.

28.A: Müllerian derivatives (uterus, tubes, upper vagina) regress under Sertoli-cell AMH; testosterone does not support them.
28.B: A 46,XY fetus with testes has no ovarian follicles; follicle development is unrelated to fetal testosterone.
28.D: The adrenal medulla derives from neural crest and develops independently of fetal testosterone.

29.A: Müllerian duct regression is mediated by AMH from Sertoli cells, not by DHT.
29.C: Thyroid development depends on transcription factors such as PAX8, NKX2-1 and FOXE1, not on dihydrotestosterone.
29.D: Aldosterone synthesis is regulated by the renin-angiotensin system and potassium via aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2), not by DHT.

30.B: Complete androgen insensitivity causes a female phenotype at birth and breast development, not virilisation, at puberty because androgen receptors are non-functional.
30.C: Classic 21-hydroxylase CAH in 46,XX causes virilisation of a 46,XX infant at birth; the stem describes a 46,XY individual undervirilised at birth.
30.D: Turner syndrome is 45,X (or variants) with female phenotype and gonadal failure, so neither 46,XY karyotype nor pubertal virilisation fits.

32.A: Complete androgen insensitivity does not virilise, and AMH from the testes causes Müllerian regression, so there is no uterus.
32.B: Menorrhagia requires a uterus and menstruation; in complete androgen insensitivity the uterus is absent and patients present with primary amenorrhoea.
32.D: Without a uterus, menarche cannot occur in complete androgen insensitivity; primary amenorrhoea is the typical presentation.

33.A: Complete androgen insensitivity occurs in 46,XY individuals with testes and causes undervirilisation, not virilisation of a 46,XX child.
33.C: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency causes undervirilisation of 46,XY individuals; it does not virilise a 46,XX child with ovaries.
33.D: Swyer syndrome is 46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis with streak gonads and female external genitalia, not a virilised 46,XX child with normal ovaries.

35.A: TSH assesses thyroid axis function and gives no information about testicular Sertoli-cell tissue.
35.B: Aldosterone reflects mineralocorticoid status (relevant to salt-wasting CAH) but not Sertoli-cell function.
35.C: HbA1c reflects average glycaemia over months and has no role in assessing gonadal function.

36.A: Electrolytes should be checked early in suspected DSD to detect salt-wasting CAH, which can be life-threatening.
36.B: Karyotype (and rapid sex-chromosome testing) is a core first-line investigation in DSD and should not be avoided.
36.D: Psychosocial support for the family is an essential part of DSD care from the outset, not something to avoid.

37.A: Delayed puberty in girls is absence of breast development by about 13 years, the opposite of early onset before 8.
37.C: Puberty is not normal at every age; onset before 8 years in girls warrants evaluation for precocious puberty.
37.D: Primary amenorrhoea refers to absent menarche by about 15 years, not early pubertal onset.

38.B: Delayed puberty in boys is lack of testicular enlargement by about 14 years, the opposite of onset before 9.
38.C: Puberty is not normal at every age; onset before 9 years in boys warrants evaluation for precocious puberty.
38.D: Primary hypogonadism is testicular failure causing absent or arrested puberty, not early pubertal onset.

39.A: Menarche is a late event, typically about 2–2.5 years after thelarche, so it is not the first sign.
39.B: Axillary hair is usually a later pubertal feature and reflects adrenal androgens rather than central (gonadotropin-driven) puberty.
39.C: Voice deepening is an androgen-driven male pubertal feature, not the first sign of central puberty in girls.

40.A: Facial hair appears late in male puberty, well after testicular enlargement.
40.B: Voice breaking occurs in mid-to-late puberty, after testicular enlargement and growth acceleration have begun.
40.D: Pubic hair alone may reflect adrenarche; in central puberty testicular enlargement usually precedes or accompanies pubarche.

41.A: About 1–3 mL is prepubertal testicular volume, not the threshold marking onset of puberty.
41.C: 15 mL is a mid-to-late pubertal volume, well beyond the onset threshold.
41.D: 25 mL represents adult testicular volume, not the onset of gonadarche.

42.B: Central puberty causes gonadal activation (testicular enlargement or breast development); prepubertal gonads argue against it.
42.C: A testicular tumour would usually enlarge or create asymmetry of the testis, and not every case of early pubic hair is tumour-related.
42.D: Delayed puberty involves absent or late pubertal signs, not early pubic hair.

46.B: Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid for salt-wasting adrenal insufficiency and does not suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.
46.C: Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism; it does not suppress gonadotropin-driven central puberty.
46.D: Androgen replacement is used to induce puberty in hypogonadal boys and would worsen, not treat, precocious puberty.

47.A: Central precocious puberty is gonadotropin-dependent with pubertal LH levels; suppressed gonadotropins indicate a peripheral source.
47.B: Constitutional delay causes late, not early, puberty and does not involve oestrogen excess.
47.C: Primary ovarian insufficiency causes low oestrogen with elevated gonadotropins, the reverse of this picture.

48.A: McCune-Albright syndrome typically causes early, gonadotropin-independent puberty, not hypogonadotropic delayed puberty.
48.B: Complete androgen insensitivity results from androgen-receptor mutations, whereas McCune-Albright is due to activating GNAS mosaic mutations.
48.D: Salt-wasting CAH is caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency (CYP21A2), not by GNAS mutations; McCune-Albright may cause Cushing syndrome but not salt-wasting.

49.A: Hypoglycaemia, hyperkalaemia and acholic stools are not a recognised triad; hyperkalaemia points to adrenal/mineralocorticoid failure and acholic stools to cholestasis, neither a feature of McCune-Albright syndrome.
49.C: Aniridia with Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma) belongs to WAGR (11p13 deletion), and hemihypertrophy to Beckwith-Wiedemann; these are tumour-predisposition syndromes, not GNAS mosaicism.
49.D: Short stature, webbed neck and coarctation of the aorta describe Turner syndrome (or Noonan), which causes gonadal failure rather than autonomous endocrine hyperfunction.

52.A: Complete androgen insensitivity occurs in 46,XY individuals with a female phenotype who present with primary amenorrhoea, not as delayed puberty in a phenotypic boy.
52.B: Classic salt-wasting CAH presents with neonatal adrenal crisis and, if undertreated, causes androgen excess with early virilisation rather than delayed puberty in a healthy adolescent.
52.D: Congenital hyperthyroidism is a rare, transient neonatal condition from maternal TRAb; it is not a common cause of pubertal delay, and it is hypothyroidism that classically delays puberty.

53.A: Hypothalamic suppression reduces GnRH drive, giving low or inappropriately normal LH and FSH, the opposite of the raised gonadotropins in this stem.
53.C: Constitutional delay is a temporary central (hypogonadotropic) state with prepubertal-range, low LH and FSH; raised gonadotropins exclude it and indicate gonadal failure.
53.D: Prolactin deficiency does not delay puberty or raise gonadotropins; it is hyperprolactinaemia that suppresses GnRH and lowers LH/FSH.

54.B: Primary gonadal failure removes negative feedback and raises LH and FSH; low or inappropriately normal gonadotropins argue against it, so 'in every case' is wrong.
54.C: Androgen excess (e.g. CAH, tumours) causes early virilisation or precocity, not delayed puberty; any gonadotropin suppression it causes is secondary, not a cause of pubertal delay.
54.D: Hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalaemia and has no role in the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis or delayed puberty.

55.A: Turner syndrome causes hypergonadotropic hypogonadism from gonadal dysgenesis with high FSH, and anosmia is not a feature.
55.B: Cushing syndrome may suppress gonadotropins and delay puberty, but it presents with weight gain, growth failure and cushingoid features, not congenital anosmia.
55.C: McCune-Albright syndrome causes gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty from GNAS activation, the opposite of congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and is unrelated to anosmia.

56.A: Complete androgen insensitivity presents with primary amenorrhoea in a girl of normal or tall stature with breast development from aromatised testosterone, not short stature with high FSH.
56.B: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency affects 46,XY individuals with atypical genitalia who virilise at puberty; it does not explain short stature and ovarian failure in a girl.
56.D: 21-hydroxylase CAH causes androgen excess with advanced bone age and early virilisation; gonadotropins are not raised from gonadal failure.

57.A: 46,XX complete gonadal dysgenesis gives a female phenotype with streak gonads and primary amenorrhoea, not a boy with testes.
57.C: Salt-wasting CAH in boys presents with neonatal adrenal crisis or later androgen excess with suppressed gonadotropins, not small testes with high FSH/LH.
57.D: Central precocious puberty causes early pubertal testicular enlargement with pubertal LH, not small firm testes from primary testicular failure.

59.A: Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalaemia and does not explain pubertal delay linked to low energy availability.
59.B: Complete androgen insensitivity is a congenital 46,XY condition presenting with primary amenorrhoea; it is unrelated to weight loss or training.
59.C: Isolated premature adrenarche is early adrenal androgen production in young children and does not cause delayed puberty.

60.A: Advanced bone age suggests sex-steroid or androgen excess (precocity, CAH, obesity), not constitutional delay, and 'always' is incorrect.
60.B: In constitutional delay bone age typically lags chronological age by about 2 years; equality with chronological age argues against it.
60.D: Bone age is useful: a delayed bone age supports constitutional delay and helps predict remaining growth potential, though it is not diagnostic alone.

61.A: A family history of late puberty is common in constitutional delay and supports rather than undermines the diagnosis.
61.C: Delayed bone age is a typical finding in constitutional delay and supports the diagnosis, though it can also occur in organic causes.
61.D: A normal examination supports constitutional delay; it is abnormal findings such as neurologic signs or systemic illness that make the diagnosis insecure.

64.A: TSH alone misses central hypothyroidism, where TSH may be low, normal or mildly raised despite low free T4.
64.B: Serum sodium may be low in hypothyroidism but is non-specific and cannot localise the defect to the thyroid or pituitary.
64.D: Random cortisol assesses the adrenal axis (relevant to check before thyroxine in hypopituitarism) but does not distinguish primary from central hypothyroidism.

65.A: Central precocious puberty accelerates growth and advances bone age; it does not cause high TSH with low free T4.
65.C: Adrenal androgen excess increases growth velocity and bone age and does not alter TSH or free T4.
65.D: Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalaemia, not poor growth with raised TSH and low free T4.

66.B: Primary hypothyroidism produces a raised TSH as the failing thyroid loses feedback; a non-elevated TSH with low free T4 points centrally.
66.C: Hyperthyroidism gives high free T4 with suppressed TSH, not low free T4.
66.D: Low free T4 is abnormal; a non-elevated TSH is inappropriate here and must not be assumed normal, though non-thyroidal illness should be considered.

68.A: Peripheral precocious puberty raises sex steroids, accelerating growth and advancing bone age.
68.B: Cushing syndrome causes growth failure with weight gain, not weight loss; the option as worded describes no recognised entity.
68.D: Isolated premature adrenarche causes mild growth acceleration with normal or mildly advanced bone age, not poor growth with delayed bone age.

70.B: Isolated premature adrenarche causes early pubic hair or body odour only and does not cause central hypothyroidism or hypoglycaemia.
70.C: Primary aldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalaemia and does not affect TSH, GH or ACTH axes.
70.D: Simple obesity is associated with normal or increased height velocity, not central hypothyroidism and hypoglycaemia.

71.A: Hyperthyroidism does not cause micropenis or hypoglycaemia; in hypopituitarism central hypothyroidism is the expected thyroid finding.
71.B: Physiological jaundice is unconjugated and benign; prolonged jaundice in hypopituitarism is often cholestatic, and jaundice alone does not explain micropenis with hypoglycaemia.
71.C: Premature adrenarche occurs in mid-childhood with early pubic hair and is not a neonatal cause of micropenis or hypoglycaemia.

72.A: A chest X-ray is not standardised for skeletal maturity and does not estimate bone age.
72.B: A urine dipstick screens for glycosuria or proteinuria and gives no information on skeletal maturation.
72.D: An ECG assesses cardiac rhythm and conduction and has no role in estimating skeletal maturity.

73.A: Axillary odour results from adrenal androgens and occurs in adrenarche without HPG-axis activation.
73.C: Acne is androgen-driven and can occur with adrenal androgens alone, so it does not distinguish gonadarche from adrenarche.
73.D: Pubic hair can result from adrenal androgens alone in adrenarche; testicular enlargement (4 mL or more) marks true gonadarche.
